content: An oscilloscope in an electronic testing lab Uwe Moser/Alamy Microwaves seem to be able to spend “imaginary time” inside a material, but this bizarre phenomenon has never been shown to correspond to something real and measurable in the lab – until now. When a pulse of radiation, such as microwaves or light, travels through a material, the interaction with the material’s atoms can slow it down, creating a time delay. In 2016, a team of researchers calculated that this time delay can be imaginary – crunch the numbers and you get a number of seconds multiplied by the square root of -1, or the imaginary number called i . We don’t encounter such numbers in nature, but Isabella Giovannelli and Steven Anlage at the University of Maryland have found a way to measure them in an experiment anyway. “It’s sort of like a hidden degree of freedom that people ignored,” says Anlage. “I think what we’ve done is bring it out and give it a physical meaning.” The researchers sent a microwave pulse through a set of coaxial cables whose ends were connected to form the shape of a ring. They had lots of control over the pulse that entered this ring, and they very precisely collected and analysed the microwave pulse that came out. The team used an oscilloscope and other devices to determine not just how long it lingered in the cables, but also how its other properties, such as frequency, changed. They found that so-called imaginary time manifests as one tiny physical change. Microwaves are not spending an impossible amount of time in the cables; they are just jiggling through it at a slightly shifted frequency. This is because the energy and intensity of the microwaves are changing as they travel and interact with the cables’ interior, says Konstantin Bliokh at Donostia International Physics Center in Spain, who worked on the 2016 calculation. Imaginary time delays have been ignored in past experiments because researchers assumed that they are non-physical. Giovannelli says these small frequency shifts are also really difficult to detect. “It was very challenging. Part of the reason we were able to even measure this was because we have some of the best oscilloscopes in the world,” she says. Franco Nori at RIKEN in Japan, who was also involved in the 2016 work, says the new experiment is “original, thoughtful, carefully executed and important”. He and his colleagues had experimentally tested only the real – non-imaginary – part of the process, so Anlage and Giovannelli’s work completes the picture of how materials can sculpt pulses of radiation. “Several decades ago, these effects were considered as tiny, but now they play important roles in nanoscience,” says Bliokh. If generalised to include more complex systems, they could be leveraged in some sensing devices, he says. Nori says the results could also help improve devices that use light for storage, as some computer memories do. The team now plans to explore how the frequency shifts they measured relate to the way information-carrying pulses, such as those used for communication, can get corrupted as they travel through materials. “It’s like a hammer that we’ve invented, and now we can find nails,” says Anlage.

content: The feeling of riding on two wheels is unlike anything else, and vintage bikes can make the experience even more special. Even better, motorcycles are generally more affordable and easier to store than cars. This means picking up a bike for the first time, or just looking to try a different type for a bit, can be done without breaking the bank. Don’t believe us? Here are six motorcycles that can be had in #3 (good) condition for less $4000, according to our motorcycle price guide, the latest update of which went live this month. Early 1980s Harley-Davidson XLH eBay/Sam's Classic Print Ads And Tools Harley-Davidson motorcycles have an undeniable presence and always offer riders something unique. Riding one for a while is an experience worth having, especially when it’s possible to get one of the most true-to-form Harleys for under $4K. An early 1980s XLH is simple, durable, and fun. That makes sense from a brand that was just coming out from under the AMF ownership that did few favors to HD’s reputation or image among enthusiasts. The 1984-and-on models got significant updates, but those come with a premium that might not make sense if a 45-degree V-twin providing the soundtrack to an evening ride is all you need. 1976–77 Honda GL1000 Honda Early Goldwing models were a little misunderstood. Honda put the GL lineup out first and seemingly afterward decided what the bike was actually going to be. The wire-spoke GL1000s are more cafe racer than touring bike, and when thinking that way it’s easy to end up sidetracked by CB models, but those are priced accordingly for the few survivors and the heaps of hacked-up project bikes. Instead, the small weight penalty of stepping up to a GL1000 will disappear once the durability and low-maintenance engine gets you underway. These bikes are ready for anything you want to do. Find one with a fairing for a great backroad touring machine, or an un-faired model for a do-it-all standard with smooth power. 1967–76 Yamaha AT/DT Yamaha Who could talk about affordable fun without mentioning a two-stroke enduro? Certainly not us. Yamaha’s addition of street-legal gear to one of its off-road models created a fun bike that enables chasing adventure down just about any road, path, or trail you can find through the glare on your visor. The AT model features a simple and spunky 125cc engine, while the DT packs 246 cc of power. The engines are not the story, though, as the suspension and gearing encouraged riders to explore and ride new places. These bikes could do the same for you. 1990s Honda VFR750 Interceptor Honda Sporty machines of the 1990s have been heating up for long enough that many of the obvious favorites have accelerated right out of affordable fun territory. Luckily, a few models are hiding in plain sight, and they provide not only great value but a great riding experience with interesting technical features. Honda’s VFR750 features an elegant single-sided swingarm and alloy bodywork that hides a smooth-running V-4, of which Cycle World wrote: “Its torque output is so strong and consistent that the actual powerband is almost impossible to detect.” A comfortable and capable machine with retro flavor that can run with modern traffic: Who could ask for more? 1963–70 BSA A50 BSA If your version of fun is about tinkering in the garage in addition to riding, a vintage BSA twin is right up your alley. Although these are not nearly as needy as some would have you believe, it is best to be prepared and have tools handy if a #3 condition Brit bike is on your shopping list. The thrum from the exhaust when one of these is running right is a special sound, and regardless of your motorcycle interests, it should be experienced at some point. With lots of knowledge and club support out there for vintage Brit twins, it has never been easier to make a fun statement pulling into cars and coffee. 1969–70 Suzuki T350 Suzuki Two-stroke street bikes are all but dead, but for under our price point you can experience the heyday of these engines. Suzuki calls the T350 a “high-speed touring” model, and based on the double-cradle steel frame and six-speed transmission, it would be a comfortable and approachable bike for riders of all skill levels. Larger cooling fins help keep the air-cooled twin under melting point, even during extended steady-throttle cruising where most two-strokes struggle. Get some oil-burning character in your life without going all the way to a pipe-y, high-strung race replica. And they are pretty classy looking, too. The post 6 Fun Motorcycles You Could Be Riding for Less Than $4000 appeared first on Hagerty Media .

content: So it’ll be one more year for IndyCar’s Dallara DW12 chassis , which has already been in service for 14 years, certainly making it the oldest platform used in a major auto racing series. IndyCar had promised that a new car would debut for the 2027 season, but that has been postponed until at least 2028, according to the Indianapolis Star and Racer.com. Why? Not so much because the car itself couldn’t be ready, but because engine suppliers Honda and Chevrolet need more time to develop upgraded powerplants, which include a new engine and energy recovery system. Justin Casterline/Getty Images Justin Casterline/Getty Images According to Racer, the two companies need at least 18 months to build and test 50 new engines each, the quantity that is required to supply the series. Apparently, the Roger Penske–owned IndyCar series has yet to give Chevrolet and Honda a final draft of the rules governing the new engines. The current formula—a 2.2-liter, twin-turbocharged V-6, used by both Honda and Chevrolet—dates back to 2012. A hybrid system was added late last season and has earned mixed reviews from drivers and teams. Current supplier Dallara will also build the new car, currently called the IR-27. It’s unclear if it will be renamed the IR-28 … or beyond. The post Reports: New IndyCar and Engines Promised for 2027 Will Be Delayed appeared first on Hagerty Media .

content: Ford’s bonkers Mustang GTD is the pony car at its absolute wildest. The winged wonder has ultra-high-tech suspension , a thundering 815-hp supercharged 5.2-liter V-8 , and the current crown of fastest American car to lap the Nürburgring (6:52.072, in case you were wondering.) But all that prestige and performance comes at a cost—early reports on the maximum Mustang had the starting price near $300K, but that number was rumored to have ballooned to $325K as the car’s arrival drew nearer. Ford Now, we know the official starting price: $327,960. Car and Driver was the first to publish the news, after the outlet discovered one GTD owner who had posted his window sticker (aka Monroney) on a forum earlier this week. The original Facebook post can be found here . Ford The Monroney offers a pretty interesting breakdown of how the Mustang GTD is priced. According to the sticker, a Mustang GTD carries a base price of $318,760, but you have to factor in the $3700 gas guzzler tax and a hefty destination/delivery fee of $5500—both unavoidable fees, therefore factored into the out-the-door base price—to reach that figure above. The document also offers a glimpse of what some options on the GTD will cost. The exposed carbon-fiber roof tacked on $10,000, while the red painted brake calipers added another $1500. Both options are going to look fantastic on this example, which wears frozen white exterior paint. This owner opted out of the Spirit of America special edition , so we’re still uncertain how much that particular option will run. Mustang GTD Spirit of America Ford All told, this GTD owner ended up with an MSRP of $339,460. That’s steep, but we’re going to hold off on saying that it’s too much money for the car until we’ve had a chance to experience its performance for ourselves. It’s worth the investment for a number of Mustang and supercar die-hards, however; the first two years of GTD production have already been spoken for , a Ford spokesperson confirmed to Hagerty in September of last year. The post Mustang GTD to Start Just North of $325K appeared first on Hagerty Media .

content: DaysofPal – Six major European countries, along with the European Union’s top foreign affairs official, issued a joint statement on Thursday urging an immediate ceasefire in Gaza, the unimpeded entry of humanitarian aid, and the release of Israeli captives. The statement, signed by the foreign ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland, and the United Kingdom, alongside EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, followed a high-level security meeting in Rome, the UK Foreign Office reported. The gathering also included NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha, with discussions centered on European-Atlantic security and the war in Ukraine. However, the Gaza crisis took center stage in the final communiqué. In the joint statement, the ministers stressed the urgent need to cease hostilities in Gaza, resume humanitarian operations without delay, and secure the release of all hostages. “We will strengthen our partnerships in regions that impact our security, to counter instability and foster peace and prosperity—especially in the Mediterranean, Africa, the Western Balkans, the Black Sea, and the Middle East and North Africa,” the statement read. Later the same day, the UN General Assembly overwhelmingly adopted a resolution calling for an immediate ceasefire and humanitarian access in Gaza, with 149 countries voting in favor and only 12 opposing. This diplomatic effort follows an earlier call on May 16, when leaders of seven European nations—Spain, Norway, Iceland, Ireland, Luxembourg, Malta, and Slovenia—urged Israel to negotiate in good faith to end what they called a “genocidal war” against Gaza. These leaders also firmly rejected any plans for forced displacement or demographic change in the Palestinian territory. Since March 2, 2025, Israel has fully sealed all Gaza crossings, blocking humanitarian aid despite hundreds of trucks stalled at the borders. The closure has deepened Gaza’s famine, pushing the population into catastrophic conditions. With unwavering U.S. backing, Israel’s assault on Gaza—launched on October 7, 2023—has resulted in over 183,000 Palestinians killed or wounded, the majority being women and children. More than 11,000 remain missing, presumed buried under rubble or detained in unknown locations. The campaign has also caused mass displacement and widespread starvation, drawing growing international condemnation. Despite these calls for restraint and accountability, pressure is mounting on the EU and its member states to move beyond rhetoric and take concrete action to halt the atrocities and ensure humanitarian protection for Gaza’s civilian population.

content: A pair of Cadillacs will start tomorrow on the front row of the 2025 24 Hours of Le Mans, you say? Great! But don’t get too carried away with the idea that an American brand could take the overall win, which has only happened four times in nearly a century, all with Ford, the last coming in 1969. That caveat comes from, of all people, JOTA Cadillac driver Sebastien Bourdais, who held a rather gloomy press conference at Le Mans this week, where Bourdais essentially said that he’s hoping not so much for an overall win, but perhaps a top-five finish. Understandably, Cadillac public relations chose to overlook that press conference as it seeks to position dominance in qualifying with potential dominance in the real race. French driver Sébastien Bourdais signs autographs. Bruno Vandevelde/Getty Images I began covering Bourdais in 2004 when he raced for the famed Newman-Haas team in the new Champ Car World Series, born that year from what was left of CART. With McDonald’s as his sponsor, Bourdais won half the races that year, and he was essentially unchallenged for the championship through 2007 (but we shouldn’t forget that current NASCAR Cup driver AJ Allmendinger managed three straight wins in 2006). Bourdais has always been serious, even dour, when talking about his team’s chances, regardless of the series. He is also very often correct. A native of Le Mans, France, there’s nothing Bourdais would like more than an overall win at the 24 Hours. He first entered his hometown race in 1999, which was my first year at Le Mans. He came close to an overall win driving for the factory Peugeot team with three second-place finishes, and in 2016, co-drove the then-new Ford GT to a GTE Pro class win in the much-publicized Ford vs. Ferrari rematch from 50 years before. For Saturday’s start, team JOTA Cadillacs will be on the front row, with Bourdais’ teammate, Earl Bamber, qualifying second. The typically dominant Ferraris and Toyotas are back in the field, with the fastest Ferrari in seventh, Toyota in 10th. Bourdais himself was fastest in the first post-qualifying practice session. But, Bourdais said in that aforementioned press conference, he’s convinced Ferrari and Toyota are sandbagging—not showing their hand. “I think they’re making fun of us,” Bourdais said. “Honestly, a top-five would be really nice. If we ended up on the podium, it would be a bit incredible. But winning would be really unexpected.” Adding to his concern about Ferrari and Toyota is Porsche, which qualified third and fifth, and BMW, which qualified fourth and sixth. The other two Cadillacs, by the way, qualified eighth and 14th. Porsche “It’s easy to forget Porsche, with three cars that have been very, very fast on the straights since the start of the week,” Bourdais said. “We can see that they’re not far off in terms of performance, so they’ll do really, really well in the race too. BMW hasn’t been on fire the way they were last year in quali, but they’ll be very fast in the race, too.” (Very) long shots for an overall win are Alpine, Peugeot, and the plucky new Aston Martin effort. Bolstering Bourdais’ pessimism is that a Ferrari and a Toyota were fastest in the second practice session, so we’ll see. There are 21 entries in the top Hypercar class, a very strong field. The Ferraris have been so dominant the last two years—and the Toyotas for five straight years before—any winner besides those two brands would be a surprise. Ferrari Toyota In the LMP2 class, the TDS Racing entry from France will start up front, but our attention will be focused on the third-quickest car of the 17 that qualified: The AO by TF car of Louis Deltraz, Dane Cameron, and amateur racer and team principal P.J. Hyett, a 41-year-old software developer. If that team name doesn’t ring a bell, this might: It’s the Spike the Purple Dragon car that runs here in the IMSA series. “It was a special lap I’ll remember for a long time,” Hyett said, who qualified the car. Spike, U.S. fans likely know, is a teammate of Roxy, the pink dinosaur Porsche, which races in the GT class. The cartoon livery of the two cars has made them major fan favorites, with those fans buying a massive number of souvenirs. 24h Le Mans In the LM GT3 class, the top qualifier is the number 27 Heart of Racing Aston Martin, which finished third at this year’s Rolex 24 at Daytona. In all, 62 cars will be competing at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, with 186 drivers. And while there are many uniquely American storylines to follow—among them, Porsche team owner Roger Penske, 88, looking for his first overall Le Mans win, the only trophy he’s never been able to win—if you are looking for American drivers, you’ll have to look hard. Penske’s Porsches have none. Porsche Of the 63 drivers in the Hypercar class, only two are American: Brothers Jordan and Ricky Taylor, driving for their father, Wayne, in the family Wayne Taylor Racing Cadillac. There are five other teams represented as American—both Aston Martin Heart of Racing cars, both Cadillac Hertz Team JOTA cars, and the Whelan Action Express Cadillac—but none of them have an American driver. A couple of weeks ago, via a Zoom interview, I asked the three Taylors why there are so few American drivers. “I’m actually surprised, just as you are, that we don’t have more,” Ricky said. Wayne, a native of South Africa who drove to a win at Le Mans in 1998, said that manufacturers and teams want drivers with Le Mans experience, which many top American drivers simply don’t have. “If you’re going to pick someone to go to Le Mans and you’re going to want to win and represent a big brand, you can’t take a risk putting somebody in the car that’s not been there before because there’s so many things that happen. (L-R) Jordan, Ricky and Wayne Taylor, June 6, 2025, Le Mans. Bruno Vandevelde/Getty Images “Number one, the track is so big and so long that I know that when I won it in the Ferrari in the Prototype class, at one point in the race it was raining on one side of the track and completely dry on the other side of the track. These are the kinds of experiences that drivers have to have.” Le Mans is 8.467 miles, while the longest IMSA track is Road America in Wisconsin, is less than half that length. “I would say that the World Endurance Championship and IMSA drivers are probably all the top drivers in the world in terms of sports car racing,” Wayne said. “And if you’re going to go into your first Le Mans with a new manufacturer, you want to go with drivers who have the experience and understand exactly what it takes not only in the car, but the amount of stuff that they have to do during the course of the week with practice and PR events and stuff like that. I can remember this as a driver: By the time I’d get to the start of the race, I felt like I’d done a 24-hour even before I started.” The #101 Cadillac WTR, Cadillac V-Series.R of Ricky Taylor, Jordan Taylor, and Filipe Albuquerque. James Moy/Getty Images Jordan Taylor has a class win at Le Mans, coming in 2015 in a Chevrolet Corvette (there are no American drivers in the three Corvettes entered this year). “From an American driver’s perspective, there’s no better way to go than competing with Cadillac. So, for us, it’s super special to be there representing our country and the brand. When they raise the flag and play the anthem at the end of the race there, it’s very special. It’s something every driver dreams of.” For the record, of the 123 drivers in the other two classes, there are eight Americans in LMP2, and four in GT3. So 14 out of 186. The 24 Hours of Le Mans starts Saturday at 4 p.m. local time. TV coverage begins at 9 a.m. on Max and MotorTrend TV. content: After nearly two decades of faithfully driving my beloved BMWs, the day inevitably came when I knew I had to let go. They’d been excellent companions, providing memorable journeys, artistic driveway oil stains, and lasting relationships with many, many mechanics. However, their persistent quirks and occasional ABS lights, plus the undeniable allure of modern automotive comforts like Bluetooth audio and functional rear windows, made clear it was finally time for something fresh and new-to-me. I’m also about to hit a significant parenting milestone, as my teenage son races toward his full driver’s license in late September. Neither BMW—one a 23-year-old convertible, the other a 500-hp 335i—would be a reasonable “first car” for a kid, for a multitude of reasons. Thankfully, he has his heart set on our 17-year-old, weirdly reliable Range Rover, with which he is most familiar. Like most of us at his age, the waiting game for a license has turned into nervous excitement, which has manifested itself in questions and in a deep curiosity about what happens after the BMWs leave our garage. My son has always leaned into car enthusiasm. When he was young, we read car magazines at bedtime. We play identification games during road trips, and make up human names and backstories for certain cars that stand out to us. “That little truck looks like a Craig. Maybe a Steve?” one of us will quip. There’s never really a good reason; you just kinda know when you see them. Despite my long history with cars, my only experience as a seller was when I sold my grandfather-in-law’s mediocre Ford Fusion to Carvana for a lot of money. (A thing, to this day, I do not feel bad about .) Brandises are adept at buying cars, but getting rid of them? We’ve not been so great at that. I’ve not kept every car, but I’ve always replaced cars via dealership trade-ins—simple, no-nonsense transactions where my once-adored vehicles quietly and unceremoniously disappear in exchange for convenience. Because of that, my understanding of the private-sale process was firmly stuck in the past, when people placed ads on Craigslist, AutoTrader, or simply put the classic orange and black “For Sale” sign on their dashboards, which led to strangers calling strangers on the telephone. For about four months, I plyed these prehistoric methods without a nibble of real interest, yet the spam messages flowed like oil from my 335i’s rear main seal. “Hey, I like the item you’re selling and want to come see it. Will you call me at this weird phone number that begins with +54?” “I’m in Australia and can’t do a wire transfer because reasons. Can we do everything via PayPal?” For me, this is when the convenience factor of a no-nonsense dealer trade becomes most appealing and hardest to resist. Facebook Marketplace One day while getting Chinese take-out, I spotted it, in the back of a small used-car dealership on the side of a highway in my beach town locality of Wilmington, North Carolina: a red Jaguar XF-S SportBrake. The wagon was tucked away in the back of the lot, seemingly forgotten amongst a sea of Nissan Altimas and indiscernible Subaru crossovers. Whether it’s your thing or not, the SportBrake is one of those “holy crap” cars. Only 250 are reported to have sold in the United States, so to see one at a sleepy roadside lot, bereft of fanfare, was surreal. Not appreciated on our side of the Atlantic, some American-market SportBrakes languished and bounced around the lots of Jaguar Land Rover dealers for two-plus years before they were finally sold. Many examples were still covered by their six-year/60,000-mile warranties well into 2024. Jaguar The next day I popped in for a test drive and a chat with a salesman. From my internet sleuthing, I knew that the car, a 2018, had been on that lot for well over 120 days. It had been in what Carfax detailed as a minor front-end accident without any airbag deployment, and was wholesaled via trade-in from a Raleigh Porsche dealer. I had also quickly and quietly arranged an PPI with my local independent JLR experts at EuroTek. They gave me an inspection report that was the equivalent of what I’d consider a B+. A small coolant leak, which could have been attributed to prolonged sitting , some panel-gap weirdness on the front fascia, and a few scuffs were really the only noticeable faults. Armed with that information, I played hardball. “Look, I know this car has been on your lot for a long time,” I told the salesman, like I did this sort of wheeling and dealing every day. “You’re losing money every day on interest, and I’m clearly the only guy in America who wants a red Jaguar station wagon with a flamboyant red interior and a minor coolant leak.” “We can do the deal if I can get both of those BMW’s for $5000,” the salesman shot back. Oof. Kelley Blue Book had estimated my Blinkerless of BMWs (my new name for a group of Bimmers) at about $8000 apiece. My emotional connection to the cars wouldn’t allow me to let go of them for less than $10,000. When it came to negotiating trades, my attachment to the cars was a weakness, but it would later prove a bonus for my wallet. Jaguar The salesman and I texted back and forth for weeks. (Somehow, the conversation grew to include a mutual friend of ours. Small towns, y’all.) I continuously reminded the salesman that the beginning of the month was coming and that every extra day the SportBrake spent on that lot was costing him money. Finally, he told me that a gentleman from New York was interested in the car. The guy wanted to snag it before the end of the week, he said, so I’d better come get it quick. Pffft. Clearly a bargaining ploy by a seasoned salesman. I decided to wait, and call his bluff. Friday came and went, and I stealthily strolled by the lot like an awkward teenager obsessed with his crush. The car was gone. In a world where every dealer price is automatically set and controlled by constantly changing market conditions and publicly available sale prices, I realized the real game was how much I was willing to lose on my trade-ins. My bluff had been called. The salesman was clearly relieved. “Hey man, I’m sorry but that fella from New York really liked it,” he told me. “You’ll get a kick out of this—it’s gonna be his new farm truck.” Jaguar Deflated, and sorry for the poor Jaguar, I moved on. I was glad my son hadn’t watched me play hardball for a car I really wanted only to get denied. I tried to look on the bright side: After all, I got to spend a fun day leisurely test-driving the long red wagon all over town. I could brag that I drove .4% of every Jaguar SportBrake ever brought to the States, and probably well over 1% of those cars that are still on the road. That was kinda neat, big picture. I looked around in the following weeks and found a couple SportBrakes in less than fantastic shape. A gray one in Florida with a salvage title had been available for over a year due to flooding. A model in black had suffered serious driver’s side damage but, since the accident, had been returned to an impressive state of repair. (Always search for photos using the car’s VIN, folks.) Another seller, in San Francisco, was advertising a black example for which he wanted double the market value. Like the Facebook Marketplace inquiries, these cars were all individual lessons for my teenager, but one in particular helped make it “click” for him. We had found a dealer in Texas who had a SportBrake in silver with chrome trim. Good wheels, very clean interior. Its mileage was noticeably lower than that of the others, but something wasn’t quite right. Jaguar “You see that little square hole on the front bumper?” I asked my son. “That’s where the tow ring attaches to the frame. Since it’s missing, the car was likely being towed recently and unable to move under its own power. I know it sounds trivial, but we need to ask about that,” I explained in true dad fashion. Most of the time, Dad giving you a “well actually” fact leads to teenage eye-rolling, but this time it led to follow-up questions—and a fact-finding mission. Sure enough, that missing cap led to an awkward conversation with a very nervous salesman. The engine, he admitted, “isn’t actually in the car right now, but is being rebuilt by a guy who knows those things.” He couldn’t explain the reason for the rebuild and was not forthcoming with any service records. It felt good to be back on the other side of the bluff, and it was a solid opportunity to show my son that taking a few seconds to inquire about a seemingly innocuous detail can save you a world of trouble. Disappointed, I refocused my search. Eventually, I found a very clean, well-equipped 2017 Range Rover HSE at my local JLR store for a solid price. (My mantra of “I’ll only buy sub-$25K cars” has served me well since I left college, and I remain true to it.) Strangely, Land Rovers have been the most reliable and trouble-free vehicles I have ever owned. Land Rover is my comfort brand, and it was easy to circle back to an old friend who had never let me down. My only reservation was that the Rover didn’t have the quirkiness I had envisioned for life post-BMW. Land Rover For once in my life, I settled for the mature, economical, and reasonable choice. “Hashtag-growth,” I told my son, explaining why I didn’t hold out for the 510-hp supercharged V-8. “The HSE has the same, very tuneable supercharged V-6 as the SportBrake, and it’ll be fine. I’ll do the pulleys, intake, and some other stuff and it’ll be fine.” -whispers under breath- Totally fine. After signing the paperwork for the Land Rover, and failing yet again to secure a deal that included my Snobbery of Bimmers (okay, maybe I like this one better) for trade plus cash, hope appeared in the form of my longtime friend Matt Maeken, an expert sales guide from Cape Fear Land Rover . He suggested I try listing the BMWs on Facebook Marketplace. “Man, that’s how people are selling cars now. I know you hate Facebook, but there’s money on the table and you should go get it.” Having avoided Facebook for about a decade, the idea of returning felt akin to Geraldo opening Al Capone’s vault: uncertain, oddly thrilling, and totally unpredictable. That night, I listed both cars. I wrote the most honest listings that two Marketplace Bimmers could have ever had and boosted visibility through a few cheap, sponsored posts. Over the following weeks, Marketplace provided endless entertainment. My teenage son, particularly intrigued, eagerly tracked the bizarre and colorful trade offers—guns, vintage baseball cards, decrepit vehicles—and amusing inquiries that flooded our inbox. “No, I won’t sell just the wheels. Then I won’t have any wheels.” “I’m really sorry that your grandma died …” “It sucks that your tuition is high but I don’t think we can’t work out a payment plan on this 22-year-old BMW that I’m selling privately.” Facebook Marketplace Facebook Marketplace Facebook Marketplace Facebook Marketplace Facebook Marketplace Facebook Marketplace We laughed at the absurdities and shook our heads at improbable trade offers. Each peculiar interaction offered teaching opportunities, leading to discussions about dealership convenience versus the potential financial upsides of selling a car privately, how dealers use credit to keep their lots full, and where to find the information you need to be most informed about the car you wish to purchase. Eventually, both BMWs found new homes with excited and equally improbable owners from different sides of the state. As I lamented each sale’s “hassle” to any family member who’d listen, my son soaked in the details of every notary signature and check verification, plus a weird bank policy that required multiple bankers to authenticate what I finally felt like was an acceptable amount of cash per BMW. It dawned on me that, when I was my son’s age, my parents had shielded me from all car transactions, for better or for worse. Selling a car is one of those things you don’t really think to teach your kids when they’re young—but by including them in the experience, you could help them save significant amounts of money as adults. My kid knew how to sell a car. Of course, I didn’t stop browsing. A few months into my BMW retirement, I hit a dry spell. I had gone through all of the local offerings without finding any spark of joy. After randomly adding another 20 miles to the search radius on whichever site had caught my attention that week, I found a thing—a beautiful, white 2018 Jaguar XF-S SportBrake, located in the Charlotte-adjacent town of Belmont, North Carolina, roughly 200 miles from our home. It had been there for months. Facebook Marketplace It was a single-owner car, with meticulous JLR dealer maintenance records. The listing was clear and concise. Everything about it suggested the owner knew what they were getting into when they bought a new, low-production Jaguar. After a quick call with the seller, the wagon turned out to be one of those warrantied examples that had just crossed the mileage threshold. Thanks to the service history provided by the seller, I knew that all of the usual JLR V-6 trouble-spots had been addressed, under warranty, before they became an issue. I enthusiastically showed the listing to my wife and son. Whether equally smitten, tired of my hunting, or eager to snag the newly acquired Land Rover, my wife declared, “You need to go get this car.” Conveniently, my son’s spring break had just begun, and he was lamenting the lack of any memorable trip on our yearly calendar. On impulse, we decided that acquiring this Jaguar would become our 2025 spring-break father-son adventure. I came up with a reasonable offer that was slightly lower than asking but still within my used-car buying parameters (never over $25K). I shared it with the seller, and we met in the middle, on a mutually agreeable price. Darwin Brandis Two days later, my son and I boarded an early morning flight to the Gateway to Gastonia (also known as Charlotte, North Carolina) with our wallets, a bank check, and sheer optimism. No luggage, no backup plan—just excitement. “New car day is like the best day,” my son exclaimed as we settled into our economy seats near the lavatory. “Let’s not get too overly excited,” I said, trying to hide my own excitement. “We’re kind of taking a leap with this one. Hopefully this whole thing will be legit.” My college roommate, now a local legend of a high school math teacher, had agreed to collect us from the airport and drive us to our rendezvous point—a Belmont bank with which he was familiar. My son was first to spot the bright-white, elongated Jaguar. Darwin Brandis “Dad there it is! It’s happening!” he exclaimed with joy. “New car day is the best day,” I thought to myself. “I’m real!” I excitedly announced out the window to the sellers, who had proven equally courageous in their own leap of faith, and were relieved to see us. After a few laps around the exterior, and an obligatory start of the engine, we moved inside the bank, where the formalities began. My son watched every nuance. When the notary requested the mileage for the title, I instructed the young man to head outside and check the odometer. Moments later, he returned sheepishly. “Y’all, I was so excited about the car that I forgot to look—I just sat in the driver’s seat and admired the interior.” Darwin Brandis With the purchase made, the next task was registration. As we got ready to drive to a nearby shopping mall that housed the nearest DMV, everyone suddenly realized it was Good Friday—in North Carolina, a government holiday. (That explained why my teacher friend wasn’t at work!) We came up with a new plan to drive the 200 miles home on the seller’s personalized, North Carolina mountain-themed license plate, promising its safe return once registration was completed the following Monday. Through this process, my son watched carefully, absorbing lessons on trust, negotiation with unfamiliar people, and business improvisation. Our return trip became a leisurely exploration of our new car. We acquainted ourselves with the Jaguar’s InTouch infotainment system, luxurious ride quality, and impressive multi-modal transmission settings. With every mile traveled, we learned that the patience that paid off when we found this car was just as important as the patience we had needed to sell the BMWs. Darwin Brandis Later, reflecting on our adventure, I recognized a key reason I’d amassed vehicles over the years: I had been reluctant to confront the modern and newly social method of selling cars on my own. The experience of selling the BMWs showed me that selling through social media wasn’t nearly as intimidating as I’d believed it to be. In fact, my son and I made it humorous. Facebook Marketplace messages were something we looked forward to checking every evening. More importantly, beyond the joy of finally acquiring a coveted car, this entire episode evolved into a meaningful bonding experience with my son. My hope is that he’ll carry forward not only fond memories of our spontaneous road trip but also a practical, empowering realization: Cars don’t sell themselves, and putting in a little effort, patience, and care can reap substantial rewards. It’s a valuable lesson in responsibility and autonomy, wrapped neatly in an unforgettable, serendipitous father-son adventure. As for the name of our new car? content: Colombia will host an emergency meeting of the so-called Hague Group in July to denounce Israel’s “genocide” in Gaza, Palestine. Credit: Unknown , Public Domain / Rawpixel. Colombia is preparing to host an emergency meeting of the so-called Hague Group countries in one month to address what it calls the “genocide” in Gaza, Palestine. Convened by Colombia and South Africa, the Foreign Ministers of the eight member countries—Bolivia, Colombia, Cuba, Honduras, Malaysia, Namibia, Senegal, South Africa—will spend two days coordinating joint responses and presenting concrete measures to demand an end what they call the “genocide” in Gaza, according to official sources. The Group was established on January 31 of this year in The Hague, Netherlands, with the goal of articulating international pressure based on legal instruments—the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ)—to combat what it calls “serious violations of international law” in Palestine. Colombia to host emergency Hague Group meeting on Gaza “genocide” On July 15 and 16, Colombia will host the emergency meeting of the so-called Hague Group to address what it calls the “genocide” in Gaza , Palestine. The objective is for these countries to define and announce concrete measures so that coordinated action can end the situation in the Gaza Strip, which they denounce as a genocide committed by the Israeli military . According to a statement from Colombia’s Foreign Ministry, “the emergency meeting is convened in response to Israel’s ongoing and escalating violations of international law in the occupied Palestinian territory, including the crime of genocide.” Additionally, the statement notes that “the meeting will focus on coordinated legal and diplomatic measures to end these serious violations.” With participation from founding member countries, as well as non-member states of the Hague Group, the emergency meeting will focus on states’ legal obligations—as determined in the International Court of Justice’s (ICJ) July 2024 Advisory Opinion—to end all actions “that contribute to maintaining the illegal situation created by Israel in the occupied Palestinian territory” and to safeguard the full realization of the Palestinian people’s inalienable right to self-determination. The death toll in Palestine exceeds 55,000, most of them children. Credit: Ashraf Amra , UN, CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia. The Hague Group: An organization created to defend international law in Palestine Since its formation, the bloc has agreed on three measures aimed at holding the State of Israel accountable: First, supporting legal actions before the ICC and ICJ, including arrest warrants for senior officials such as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Second, implementing an arms and ammunition embargo; and finally, restricting access to national ports for ships suspected of transporting weaponry or fuel destined for Israel. The meeting in Bogoa, Colombia, represents the group’s first in-person gathering—co-chaired by Colombia and South Africa—and serves as a declaration of intent beyond diplomatic rhetoric. The host country’s government, Colombia, has been highly critical of Benjamin Netanyahu ’s administration. In fact, its president, Gustavo Petro , was among the first global voices to characterize Israel’s military response in Gaza as “genocide” following the October 2023 Hamas attacks. The Hague Group was created in January 2025 in this Dutch city to defend international law in Palestine and denounce Israeli military intervention. Credit: Pierre Crom / Getty Images. Violence continues in the region The conflict in Gaza has had a devastating toll. International organizations estimate that since October 2023, approximately 55,000 Palestinians have been killed, the majority being women and children. Furthermore, humanitarian organizations are warning of the risk of mass starvation for a population of nearly 2 million people. Concurrently, in November 2024, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former minister Gallant for war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. Then, in March 2025, South Africa formally filed a genocide case with the ICJ, supported by numerous countries in the region, including Belgium, Brazil, Chile, and Uruguay. But the violence continues to spread. Last night, the Israeli military attacked Tehran, the capital of Iran, aiming to neutralize that country’s nuclear facilities. In this operation, it killed three senior Iranian government officials, including the chief of the Revolutionary Guard, Hossein Salami. Regarding this attack, the Colombian government issued a statement this morning expressing its concern and “the potential repercussions these events could have on regional stability and international security.” Additionally, Colombia recalled that such actions “in the context of international conflicts should comply with the principles of international law, including respect for the sovereignty of States, as well as the norms of international humanitarian law for the protection of the civilian population.” The Hague Group intends to build support for these judicial initiatives, coordinating diplomatic action aligned with the recommendations of international law, including sanctions and embargoes. #COMUNICADO pic.twitter.com/aSDYZ6EtHj — Cancillería Colombia (@CancilleriaCol) June 13, 2025

content: DaysofPal – Ahead of a planned Global March to Gaza, Egyptian authorities have arrested and deported dozens of international pro-Palestinian activists to put pressure on Israel to lift its blockade of the besieged Palestinian enclave. The march, set for Friday, was expected to see thousands of activists from around the world gather in Egypt and travel to the Rafah border crossing with Gaza. Participants hoped to deliver humanitarian aid and draw global attention to what the United Nations has called “the hungriest place on Earth.” However, Egyptian authorities have launched a widespread crackdown in recent days. According to airport officials and organizers, dozens of activists were detained at Cairo International Airport and in hotels across the capital. Many were later deported without explanation. An Egyptian official, speaking anonymously to The Associated Press, confirmed that more than three dozen activists, mostly European passport holders, had been deported in recent days. “They intended to travel to Northern Sinai without obtaining required authorizations,” the official said. The crackdown intensified on Thursday, when Reuters reported that at least 73 foreign nationals were deported on a flight to Istanbul. An additional 100 were reportedly still being held at the airport awaiting deportation. Activists from around the world targeted Saif Abukeshek, spokesperson for the Global March to Gaza, told AFP that over 200 activists were either detained at Cairo airport or interrogated in their hotels. Among them were citizens from the United States, Australia, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Algeria, and Morocco. “Plainclothes officers came with lists of names, searched their belongings, and in some cases confiscated phones,” Abukeshek said. “After interrogations, some were arrested and others were released. Some have already been deported.” A group of Greek participants issued a statement saying that dozens of their members had been detained despite holding valid documents and complying with all Egyptian entry procedures. “We have broken no law and followed every legal procedure in entering the country,” the statement read. Despite the crackdown, organizers say the march will proceed as planned. “We look forward to providing any additional information the Egyptian authorities require to ensure the march continues peacefully,” the organizers said in a statement. Protesters intend to travel by bus to El Arish in the Sinai Peninsula before marching roughly 50 kilometers to the Rafah border. They aim to meet a convoy of activists traveling overland from Tunisia in support of the campaign. The goal, organizers say, is to “create international moral and media pressure” to open the Rafah crossing and lift the Israeli-imposed blockade on Gaza. Israel closed all borders with Gaza in March amid its ongoing war on the territory, where more than 55,000 Palestinians have been killed, according to local authorities. Though some aid has been allowed into Gaza in recent weeks, humanitarian agencies report that the quantities are far below what is needed and that distribution is often disrupted by Israeli attacks on aid seekers. The Global March follows another recent effort to break the siege, the Madleen, a humanitarian aid ship carrying prominent figures including Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, French MEP Rima Hassan, and Al Jazeera journalist Omar Faiad. The vessel was intercepted and seized by Israeli forces earlier this week in international waters. Egypt’s stance and Israeli pressure Egypt has long maintained that its side of the Rafah crossing remains technically open but that access is blocked by Israel’s control over the Palestinian side. On Wednesday, Egypt’s Foreign Ministry reiterated that only those with proper authorization would be allowed to travel to border areas. “Egypt holds the right to take all necessary measures to preserve its national security, including the regulation of the entry and movement of individuals within its territory, especially in sensitive border areas,” the ministry said. Israeli officials have urged Egypt to prevent the march. Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant described the participants as “jihadist protesters,” claiming their presence at the border would “endanger the safety of [Israeli] soldiers and will not be allowed.” Despite mounting obstacles, Abukeshek said activists remain determined. “We are not deterred,” he told AFP. “We will continue with our peaceful mission to demand the lifting of the blockade and the opening of Rafah for the people of Gaza.” In solidarity with the Palestinian people, this Arab popular movement is gaining momentum for the first time to end the aggression against the Gaza Strip, which has been under the most brutal siege in over 17 years. Israel has reclosed all crossings into Gaza since last March and completely blocked the entry of fuel, leading to the shutdown of most hospitals, bakeries, and water desalination plants. Even UN aid has not been spared, with convoys being targeted and obstructed. Israel launched its aggression against the Gaza Strip after Operation Tufan al-Aqsa on October 7, 2023, intensifying the blockade and using starvation, thirst, and the denial of medicine as weapons against civilians.

content: DaysofPal – As the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza deepens, prominent scholars and rights advocates are calling Israel’s actions genocide and warning the international community of the broader implications. When Greta Thunberg landed in Paris on Tuesday, deported from Israel after attempting to reach Gaza in solidarity with besieged Palestinians, she didn’t mince words. “Because of racism, that’s the simple answer,” she told reporters when asked why world governments weren’t intervening to stop Israel’s blockade of the Strip. She repeatedly referred to Israel’s campaign as “genocide.” Her remarks came amid mounting pressure from legal experts, humanitarian groups, and scholars who argue that Israel’s ongoing war on Gaza, now in its 20th month, meets the definition of genocide. More than 55,000 people are estimated to have been killed, according to The Lancet . Gaza’s infrastructure has been decimated. Important humanitarian aid is still unable to enter due to a total blockade that is in place on land, in the air, and at sea. However, the majority of Western governments continue to avoid using the term “genocide,” even though many of them played a key role in creating the post-World War II legal framework intended to stop such crimes. Segal: “They believe they are outside the law” But for Dr. Raz Segal, an Israeli scholar of Holocaust and Genocide Studies at Stockton University, the debate goes far beyond semantics. “Israeli Jews are imagining that they’re fighting a colonial war against barbarians,” Segal told Middle East Eye. “They are completely thinking they are outside the law.” Segal points out that international law was originally crafted to regulate conflicts between European powers. “It was never meant to apply to colonial wars,” he explained. This legacy, he argues, has contributed to the normalization of disproportionate and destructive military campaigns against non-Western populations. Speaking at the Arab Center Washington DC’s annual Palestine conference this week, Segal emphasized the depth of Palestinian dehumanization in Israeli society. “This kind of social and political atmosphere doesn’t change quickly. It’s an intergenerational process,” he said. “In 1945, Nazi Germany is defeated. Does that mean that millions of Nazis changed their minds overnight?” The destruction in Gaza has reached extraordinary levels. Satellite imagery analyzed by Kent State University’s Dr. He Yin shows up to 98 percent of the enclave’s vegetation has been destroyed—rendering basic survival nearly impossible. In January, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) concluded it was “plausible” that Israel’s actions in Gaza violate the Genocide Convention. But Segal urges people not to get lost in legal terminology, pointing instead to the broader historical pattern of Palestinian displacement, known as the Nakba , or catastrophe. “It’s about elimination, destruction, forced displacement, and removal. About creating a greater Israel with maximum territory and minimum or no Palestinians,” he said. Legal system under threat, Callamard warns Agnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International, reinforced that message in her keynote speech at the same conference. She rejected the notion that Israel’s campaign is driven solely by military necessity. “There is absolutely no doubt that there is a genocidal intention,” Callamard said. “It is intentionally engineered. It’s not recklessness; it’s deliberate.” She also warned that the international legal system is under direct threat, citing political backlash against the International Criminal Court (ICC) after it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. The court also issued warrants for three Hamas leaders, all of whom have since been killed by Israel. Segal added that if international law is seen to apply unequally, it could collapse entirely. “International law had discarded millions of people, Palestinians among them, well before October 7,” he said. “But that doesn’t mean it isn’t worth saving.” For Segal, the only viable path forward requires dismantling the concept of a Jewish ethnonationalist state and establishing a political structure based on equality. “It needs to be a state where everyone—Jews, Palestinians, and others—have equal rights,” he said. “That’s the change of the political structure we need.” He also noted that Israeli political rhetoric over the past two years has consistently conflated Hamas with all Palestinians and blurred the lines between military operations and civilian targeting. “It doesn’t take a degree in comparative literature to see this,” he remarked. “The only way [many Israeli leaders believe] to deal with Palestinians is to destroy them.” Callamard called for immediate international action. “We must be very loud about the fact that people must fear, fear their complicity in genocide,” she said. Both Segal and Callamard warned that failure to act doesn’t just doom Gaza; it endangers the entire international legal system. “Israel’s attack on Gaza,” Segal concluded, “is becoming a model for the very small and murderous minority of people around the world.”

content: A rare collection of gold coins found in a small town in France has fetched nearly $3.5 million, stunning experts. Credit: PHGCOM / CC BY-SA 4.0 A quiet village in France has found itself in the spotlight after a hidden stash of rare gold coins was discovered in the walls of a stone house, eventually selling at auction for more than $3.48 million. The remarkable find came from the home of Paul Narce, an elderly man who lived a quiet, solitary life in Castillonnès, a small town in southwestern France. Narce, who passed away at age 89 in 2024, had no direct heirs. After his death, a notary assigned to handle his estate began a thorough inspection of his property. During that process, the notary uncovered a secret compartment behind a painting in a storage room. Inside, he found a carefully preserved collection of over 1,000 gold coins—some dating back more than 2,000 years. The collection had been meticulously organized and stored in cloth pouches, each filled with dozens of gold coins known as “Napoléons.” The coins were not only historically valuable but also extremely rare, drawing immediate interest from collectors and experts around the world. Rare gold coins span centuries and civilizations The coins reflect a wide swath of European history, with origins that stretch from ancient Greece through to 18th-century France. Among the standout pieces was a rare coin from the Kingdom of Macedonia bearing the likeness of Alexander the Great . Other highlights included gold currency from the Byzantine Empire , medieval Gaul, and coins from the French Revolution. One notable set contained seven rare coins from the 14th-century Duchy of Aquitaine, featuring the image of Edward the Black Prince. The collection also included coins from the reigns of French kings Louis XIII through Louis XVI—some minted shortly after the French monarch’s execution in 1793. Coin expert Thierry Parsy, who evaluated the collection before the sale, described it as one of the most extraordinary private holdings ever seen in France . It’s not just the number of coins, but the rarity and range that make this collection so special, Parsy said. Auctioned in Paris by Beaussant Lefèvre and Associates , the collection was expected to bring in $2.3 million but far exceeded those estimates. The final total topped $3.48 million, a figure that stunned even seasoned auction professionals. Village surprised by legacy hidden in plain sight Locals in Castillonnès, a village of just 1,300 people, were unaware of the treasure hidden within one of their quietest homes. Mayor Pierre Sicaud told Sud Ouest that Narce and his late sister Claudette were polite and reserved, never hinting at their secret passion for collecting. This was just an ordinary home near the town hall, the mayor said. No one had any idea what was inside. The notary overseeing Narce’s estate has since located distant relatives, who are now legally entitled to inherit the unexpected fortune. Curiously, this is not the first time Castillonnès has been associated with a gold discovery. In 2014, a British couple found 45 Spanish gold coins from the 1590s while renovating their home in the same village. With this latest find, the town has once again made headlines for uncovering rare treasures hidden in everyday walls.

content: A wooden coffin shaped like a boat, uncovered at a Xiaohe burial site in China’s Tarim Basin. Credit: Fan Zhang et al. / CC BY-SA 4.0 A recent archaeological review is uncovering new perspectives on one of China’s most unusual burial customs—ancient boat coffins, hidden for centuries beneath the dry sands of the Tarim Basin in Xinjiang. Led by archaeologist Dr. Gino Caspari, the study revisits a little-understood ancient community that once thrived in the region more than 3,000 years ago. These boat-shaped graves are part of the Xiaohe culture, which existed between 1950 and 1400 BCE. The Xiaohe cemetery lies in one of the driest places on Earth, yet many of its wooden structures, animal remains, and wooden poles have remained surprisingly well-preserved. The graves stand out for their distinct design—narrow wooden coffins with curved sides and flat bases, resembling small boats placed in desert pits. Caspari highlights the unique nature of these burial practices, which sharply contrast with those of neighboring societies. By examining older interpretations of the site, he aims to better understand the cultural meaning behind these carefully crafted graves. Uncovering more ancient boat graves at forgotten site Chine The Xiaohe cemetery was first recorded in the early 1900s and briefly explored by Swedish archaeologist Folke Bergman in 1934. However, it remained mostly untouched until the early 2000s when the Xinjiang Institute of Archaeology resumed full excavation. This effort uncovered 167 additional graves, adding to Bergman’s original discovery of 12. Experts believe the site may have held up to 350 burials before time and erosion took their toll. An artist’s illustration shows how the Xiaohe culture may have pictured a reversed or mirrored world after death. Credit: Anja Schorneck / CC BY 4.0 Although the scale of the cemetery is large, only a handful of graves have been studied in detail. Caspari noted that documentation of the site remains limited, with only a few maps and scattered records available to researchers. Through analysis, researchers have recognized three main styles of burial. The first, and most common, includes wooden boat-like coffins placed in sand pits, each marked by a tall wooden post. A second, more rare type, uses clay coverings over wooden coffins that contain only female remains. A third form—a rectangular setup topped with cattle skulls and hides—holds no human bodies and may have served a ceremonial or symbolic purpose. Boat coffins: Symbols of a spiritual voyage after death Caspari’s research focuses on the meaning behind the boat-shaped coffins. Some earlier studies proposed these were symbolic of boats used for a journey into the afterlife. Caspari supports this theory, pointing to their structure and the use of cattle hides, which may have helped seal and protect the coffins—possibly even mimicking ancient watercraft. Mummy from a Bronze Age cemetery at Xiaohe, Xinjiang(1500BC). By DNA test, archaeologists find the Xiaohe people had a mixed ancestry of South Siberians and West Europeans. Yet perhaps she should be left alone in her snug boat coffin, instead of being displayed in a glass case. pic.twitter.com/foKyn0U7s4 — Jin Xu 徐津 (@xujnx) November 3, 2019 He also challenges ancient beliefs about the tall wooden poles that accompany the boat coffins in China . Rather than resembling human forms, Caspari suggests they might symbolize paddles or posts used for docking, possibly to guide souls on a spiritual journey beyond death. He links these ideas with ancient beliefs about a reversed or mirrored world after death, noting similarities with early Scandinavian, Saharan, and Egyptian views of the afterlife. Despite these insights, the Xiaohe culture’s sudden disappearance around 1400 BCE remains a puzzle. Caspari admits there is not enough information to offer a solid explanation. Access to the region remains limited, making further research difficult. This lack of access is a setback, Caspari explained, because the Xinjiang region is key to understanding how ancient cultures developed and interacted across Central Asia.

content: Colombian artist Gustavo Velez opened an exhibition titled Geometria Senza Confine in Italy, running until September. Credit: Gustavo Velez Art / Instagram Colombian visual artist Gustavo Velez is currently showcasing his latest exhibition, titled Geometria Senza Confine, in Lucca, Italy. The Colombian’s works will remain on display until September 21. The region of Tuscany has become the setting for Velez’s most recent solo show, which is open to the public in the historic city of Lucca. The exhibition features a selection of 14 monumental sculptures that explore the relationship between matter, form, and movement, creating a harmonious dialogue between contemporary art and Italy’s rich cultural heritage. In addition, this year the Colombian artist will donate a monumental marble sculpture to be part of the Open-Air Museum of Pietrasanta, joining works by renowned artists such as Fernando Botero, Sophia Vari, Julio Larraz, and Park Eun Sun, among others. What is Gustavo Velez’s exhibition in Italy about? Velez’s exhibition in Lucca brings together a collection of sculptures that balance strength and subtlety, standing out for their curved lines, ascending forms, and structures that evoke a sense of perpetual motion. Created primarily in Carrara marble, bronze, and stainless steel, the sculptures are seamlessly integrated into the city’s historic setting, contrasting the modernity of their forms with Tuscany’s classical architecture. Each piece seems to float or expand in space, inviting viewers to pause and reflect on the relationship between the body, matter, and emptiness. The central theme of this exhibition revolves around constant transformation a concept that Vélez expresses through twisting, unfolding, and rising forms that serve as visual metaphors for growth, evolution, and spiritual connection. Some pieces resemble unfolding wings, while others suggest spirals of energy or stylized natural elements. Through his technical mastery and aesthetic sensitivity, Velez crafts a visual journey that offers a sensory and contemplative experience in dialogue with Tuscany’s timeless beauty and historical legacy. This is not Velez’s first time exhibiting in Italy. In 2021, he held a solo exhibition in Pietrasanta, a Tuscan town celebrated for its sculptural heritage and its proximity to the Carrara marble quarries. On that occasion, he was praised for how his artworks interacted with the town’s urban space and surrounding landscapes. Ver esta publicación en Instagram Una publicación compartida por Gustavo Vélez Escultor (@gustavovelezart) Who is Colombian artist Gustavo Velez? Gustavo Velez is a Colombian sculptor born in Medellin in 1975, internationally acclaimed for his expertise in working with materials such as marble, bronze, and stainless steel. From a young age, he showed a deep interest in art, combining his academic studies with sculpture classes at local art academies. After finishing school, he traveled to Italy to study at the Lorenzo de Medici Academy in Florence and later continued his training in the workshops of Pietrasanta, a Tuscan town famed for its marble traditions. Throughout his career, Velez has developed a distinctive visual language characterized by dynamic geometric forms that convey motion, balance, and expansion. His monumental sculptures have been exhibited in public spaces, galleries, and museums across Asia, Europe, and the Americas. He has participated in art fairs and exhibitions in cities such as Tokyo, Beijing, Seoul, London, Madrid, Miami, Mexico City, and Cartagena. His contributions to the arts have earned him prestigious honors, including Colombia ’s Order of Democracy Simón Bolívar and the Golden Star of Antioquian Culture. In 2013, Velez was selected to hold a solo sculpture exhibition in Pietrasanta known as the global cradle of sculptors where he became the youngest artist ever to intervene two of the town’s most emblematic spaces: the Piazza del Duomo and the Church of Sant’Agostino. There, he installed monumental sculptures made of bronze, steel, and marble, some reaching up to seven meters in height and weighing up to eight tons, further solidifying his position in the European art scene. Today, Velez divides his time between his workshop in Medellin where he creates steel pieces and the Carrara quarries in the Apuan Alps, where he produces his marble works.

content: A groundbreaking DNA analysis indicates that the first kings of Poland may have originated in what is now Scotland. Credit: SebbeKg – CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons. A groundbreaking DNA analysis indicates that the male line of Poland’s first kings, the Piast royal house, may have originated in what is now Scotland, rather than among local Slavic tribes. Research teams exhumed more than a dozen Piast-era crypts, including the large cemetery beneath Płock Cathedral, recovering bones dated between 1100 and 1495 that matched the dynasty’s documented timeline. Geneticists at Poznań University of Technology, led by Marek Figlerowicz, successfully extracted readable Y‑chromosome DNA from 30 men and three women believed to span the Piasts’ rule. Nearly all of the male samples carried a rare Y‑chromosome haplogroup most closely matching a Pictish burial in eastern Scotland from the 5th or 6th century. “There is no doubt we are dealing with genuine Piasts,” Figlerowicz told a May 2025 conference in Poznań. The DNA found in the environmental component shows that Poland’s first kings may have originated from Scotland The study’s environmental component reinforces the narrative of a foreign elite. Analysis of pollen cores from Lake Lednica, which is often called the cradle of the Piast state, revealed a sharp 9th‑century shift from forest to farmland and pasture, which is consistent with slash‑and‑burn agriculture to support a ruling class. Charcoal and soot layers suggest widespread fires, while complex science models of tribute, labor, and fort‑building would show the emergence and eventual decrease of fortified settlements around Gniezno and Poznań in Poland. The genetic and ecological data therefore challenge the long‑standing belief that the Piasts were purely local Slavic chiefs. Instead, they suggest the dynasty’s ancestors migrated from the North Atlantic region, likely through a dynastic marriage or small group movement centuries before Duke Mieszko I in 992 AD. Other researchers remain certain of the Piast’s Slavic origin However, critics argue the Scottish‑Piast link rests on shaky foundations. Dr. Dariusz Błaszczyk of the University of Warsaw’s Institute of Archaeology warned that the study may have misassigned the key Y‑DNA haplogroup. Błaszczyk says the Poznań team based its R1b‑S747 identification on a single sample attributed to Wacław I of Płock (1293–1336), and that the assignment is inconsistent with other data. He suggests contamination, DNA degradation, or sequencing errors could explain the anomalous result, and remains convinced that the Piasts’ male line more likely carried the U512 subclade of R1b, which is common in ancient Poland , rather than a Scottish‑linked variant. Questions over the team’s use of radiocarbon dating remain Questions also remain over the radiocarbon dating and skeletal attribution used by the team. Błaszczyk noted that the remains assigned to Władysław Herman (1044–1102) and Bolesław Krzywousty (1086–1138) showed dates in the 14th–16th centuries, raising doubts about their identity. “It may be that the bone samples do not actually belong to the rulers in question,” he said. He also urged the publication of the full data set to resolve discrepancies between researchers. Despite these critiques, the Poznań group, which is supported by Poland ’s National Science Centre, has published 16 peer‑reviewed papers since 2014 and established a public database of ancient Polish genomes. Future work, including DNA sequencing of Piast remains at Kraków’s Wawel Castle and extended pollen records back to the 7th century, may clarify whether a Scottish migrant really founded one of Europe’s most enduring dynasties.

content: Read: 2 min Mark Carney’s first months as prime minister signal a clear ambition: to make nation-shaping investments that restore Canada’s influence, economic strength and credibility on the world stage. He’s moving fast, and for good reason. It will take exactly that kind of ambition if there’s any hope of reversing the impacts of more than three decades of drastic under-investment in Canada’s global engagement. One of the things he plans to do is see Canada meet NATO’s two per cent of GDP target for defence spending — a tectonic shift in Canadian foreign policy. That’s a big step in the right direction, and I say that as someone who runs a charity and knows firsthand how many urgent priorities are competing for dollars. But defence spending alone won’t secure Canada’s place in the world. If we’re serious about global leadership, then we need to match our military ambition with equally bold investments in soft power. And that means international development. Development assistance is not something nice we do off the side of the table. It should be seen as part of our overall global engagement strategy and policy. The Liberal Party’s platform seems to reflect this. It rightly states that “we must invest in our ability to shape the world we live in, because a peaceful, prosperous world is one where Canada thrives.” But that means not just defence. It requires all four pillars of foreign relations: trade, diplomacy, defence and yes — development assistance. Fortunately, the new government has pledged to maintain aid spending — a welcome sign in a world where key allies like the U.S., U.K., France and Germany are cutting back. But stability is not the same as leadership. What’s missing is the same ambition we’re seeing on the defence side. We need a similar clear, forward-looking investment in development that matches the scale of today’s global challenges, something on the scale of the Marshall Plan after World War Two. That bold, post-war effort wasn’t just about rebuilding Europe; it was about helping to shape a new international order. The prime minister says he wants big, nation-building projects. Here’s one: reclaim Canada’s place as a global development leader — and back it with serious funding. Just as we’re mobilizing resources for military readiness, we should be launching flagship global initiatives — serious investments in climate resilience, democratic institutions and inclusive economic growth. With the G7 summit just ahead, Canada can use that global stage to show it is a country that understands that real power means pairing defence with development. After all, we cannot credibly advocate for peace and stability while neglecting the very tools that help build them. To put it another way, if we can afford two per cent of our GDP for our armed forces, we can also afford — and we need to afford — equal measures of ambition for partnership, prevention and progress on the development side of things. Canadians increasingly say we must approach the world with “our elbows up.” If that’s the case, then we need to show up with the full toolkit. Defence, yes, but also development programs that can help to prevent conflicts, build resilience, avoid crises and strengthen the global partnerships we’ll need in the tough years ahead.
